title: The suffocating seas
text: For the first time, forests are spreading across the land. Roots break rock into soil. Rain washes the nutrients into the sea. Algae bloom, die and rot, using up the oxygen. Great stretches of sea turn stagnant. Reef builders and armoured fishes die. About 70% of species are lost, in pulses over millions of years. This is the leading idea, not a settled one: cooling and volcanoes may also have played a part.
prompt:
A painting for a natural-history museum: The suffocating seas, about 372 million years ago.
Painted in the manner of Charles R. Knight (1874–1953), the American natural-history muralist: oil on canvas, confident visible brushwork, warm golden naturalistic light, soft atmospheric haze, a palette of ochres, siennas, olive greens and dusty blues, calm and dignified realism. Keep his warmth and his eye for the real world, but follow TODAY's science, not the science of his time: paint the land, water, plants and climate exactly as described here.
What happened, from the scientific evidence: For the first time, forests are spreading across the land. Roots break rock into soil. Rain washes the nutrients into the sea. Algae bloom, die and rot, using up the oxygen. Great stretches of sea turn stagnant. Reef builders and armoured fishes die. About 70% of species are lost, in pulses over millions of years. This is the leading idea, not a settled one: cooling and volcanoes may also have played a part.
Paint the moment as seen from high in the sky: a wide view of the land and sea where it happened, as they were THEN — the continents, coasts, plants and life of that time, not today's. Show only what the description says. Living things only where it names them, small, as they are reconstructed today; none where it does not.
What could not yet exist then, so must not be painted: the first trees are fern-like early trees (such as Archaeopteris); NO conifers, palms, cycads or flowering plants.
No text, labels, map lines, arrows, borders or frame.
